plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single isometric line drawing of a rectangular block subdivided into unit cells, drawn entirely in salmon-red strokes on white. The block reads as a stack of small cubes: the front face is ruled into a four-by-four arrangement of square cells, and the visible top and right-hand faces are ruled into matching grids receding from the viewer, so an interior lattice is implied throughout. Three black dimension bars with serif end caps mark the extents. A vertical bar along the left edge is labeled H, a bar beneath the lower-left edge is labeled W, and a bar beneath the lower-right edge, receding away from the viewer, is labeled C. Near the back of the top face one cell is drawn displaced from the surface, isolating a single unit cube, and a white square panel with a thin black border and a soft drop shadow floats just above it carrying the boldface letter X. Ruling the volume into addressable cells rather than drawing a smooth solid keeps every entry individually locatable by its three coordinates. The picture gives a concrete spatial reading of a three-axis tensor whose dimensions are channels, height, and width, the shape used to hold a color image.

Vertical black dimension bar with end caps and 'H' label to the left of the block
Diagonal black dimension bar with end caps and 'W' label beneath the bottom-left receding edge
Diagonal black dimension bar with end caps and 'C' label beneath the bottom-right receding edge
Floating white square label with a thin black border, soft drop shadow, and black text (visible when a cell is lifted)

interactions.label: Highlight Channel (C)
interactions.teaches: Sweeping the slider isolates a single H×W spatial sheet, revealing how a 3D tensor layers multiple 2D maps along the depth dimension.
Hovering a cell lifts it from the volume and displays its (C, H, W) index, demonstrating that every stored value has a unique 3D spatial address.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Tensor volume is H=4 (mapped to +Y, up), W=4 (mapped to +Z, screen-left receding), C=3 (mapped to +X, screen-right receding). Block spans (0,0,0) to (3, 4, 4) in world units. Cube edges are salmon-red #F27470, 2px wide. Dimension lines are solid black. The 'W' line sits at Y=-0.5, X=0, parallel to Z. The 'C' line sits at Y=-0.5, Z=4, parallel to X. The 'H' line sits at X=-0.5, Z=4, parallel to Y.
interactionPlan.notes: When channelSlice is 0, render all cubes fully opaque white with red edges. When channelSlice > 0, set cubes outside the active C-index to a low opacity (e.g., 0.15) to highlight the active slice. For cellHover, translate the targeted cube +0.75 units along Y and mount a billboarded white square label above it displaying its index, e.g., 'X(2, 3, 1)'.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for sweeping a channel slice along C; the active H by W sheet highlights one depth position at a time, showing how a color image tensor stores multiple aligned spatial maps.
- Hover over any small cube cell to reveal its (C, H, W) index and lift it like the labeled X cell; the local highlight ties one stored value to its location in the full volume.

authoredContext:
This example shows the basic concept of working with tensors and batches
for one-dimensional data, but, in vision, most of the time we will be
working with higher-dimensional tensors. For image data we typically use
four-dimensional tensors: batch $\times$ channels $\times$ height
$\times$ width; for videos we may use five-dimensional tensors: batch
$\times$ channels $\times$ height $\times$ width $\times$ time.
Three-dimensional (3D) scans have an additional depth spatial
dimension; videos of 3D data could therefore be represented by
six-dimensional tensors. As you can see, thinking in terms of
two-dimensional matrices is not quite sufficient. Instead, you should be
imagining data processing as operating on $N$-dimensional tensors,
sliced and diced in different ways. As a step in this direction, you may
find it useful to visualize tensors in 3D, as shown in
the figure.

A 3D tensor that could represent an $C \times H \times W$ color image.

discrepancies: The prominent 'X' label and its white background box on the top face are missing from the default view
The red grid lines are noticeably thinner than the thick lines in the source figure
The dimension labels (H, W, C) are smaller and less bold than in the source image
The tick marks on the dimension lines are aligned to 3D axes rather than appearing perpendicular to the lines in 2D space
evaluation.notes: The figure successfully reproduces the 3D tensor and adds excellent interactive slicing, but misses the static 'X' label and uses thin grid lines.
action_items: Add a static 'X' label with a white background and black border to the top face of the tensor, rather than only showing it on hover.
Increase the font size and weight of the H, W, and C dimension labels.
Use a fat-line technique (e.g., LineGeometry/Line2) or thin cylinders to render the red grid lines to match the bold lines in the original figure.
Adjust the dimension line tick mark vectors so they appear perpendicular to the dimension lines in screen space.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are excellent, but the missing prominent static label and specific styling discrepancies are concrete implementation issues that the generator can easily fix.

discrepancies: Labels 'W' and 'C' vertically overlap with their respective dimension lines instead of being placed cleanly below them.
The end caps on the dimension lines are drawn as thick, prominent cylinders, whereas the source has thin perpendicular tick marks.
The red grid lines forming the tensor block are noticeably thicker than in the original source image.
evaluation.notes: Excellent interactive tensor visualization with robust pedagogy, but minor layout adjustments are needed for the dimension lines and their labels.
action_items: Adjust the HTML offsets for the 'W' and 'C' labels so they sit clearly below the dimension lines without overlapping them.
Reduce the length and radius of the end cap cylinders on the dimension lines to resemble thin, subtle ticks.
Decrease the edge radius of the cylinder geometries used for the grid edges to make the tensor look less bulky and closer to the source.
